name: Latin Empire
info: A feudal Crusader state founded by the leaders of the Fourth Crusade on Byzantine lands after the sack of Constantinople in 1204, it held the city until the Nicaean recovery of 1261.

facts.founder: The leaders of the Fourth Crusade; Baldwin I (Baldwin IX of Flanders) was its first emperor
facts.successor: Byzantine Empire, restored by the Empire of Nicaea under Michael VIII Palaiologos

t: The Latin Empire was created after the crusaders captured and plundered Constantinople in April 1204, with a Catholic emperor enthroned in place of the Orthodox Roman emperors.
Venice received three eighths of the empire in the Partitio terrarum imperii Romaniae, and its podestà in Constantinople was practically independent of the emperor.
Constant war with Bulgaria and the Byzantine successor states wore the empire down until a Nicaean force of 800 soldiers took Constantinople in July 1261.
dyk: To raise money, Baldwin II stripped the lead roofs of the Great Palace and sold them, handed his only son Philip to Venetian merchants as a guarantee for a loan, and sold the relic of the Crown of Thorns.
ev: The crusaders capture and plunder Constantinople, elect Baldwin I emperor on 9 May and crown him in the Hagia Sophia on 16 May
At the Battle of Adrianople the Bulgarian tsar Kaloyan crushes the Latin knights and captures Emperor Baldwin
The Treaty of Nymphaeum recognizes Latin control of most of Bithynia and Mysia
The Latin army is defeated at the battle of Poimanenon, and Thessalonica falls to Epirus
The last Latin possessions in Asia fall to Nicaea, and a joint Nicaean and Bulgarian siege of Constantinople fails
Michael VIII Palaiologos of Nicaea wins the Battle of Pelagonia
On the night of 24/25 July Alexios Strategopoulos enters Constantinople and restores the Byzantine Empire

sections.foundation:
The Fourth Crusade had been called to retake Jerusalem, but a sequence of economic and political events led the crusader army to Constantinople. The plan had been to restore the deposed Byzantine Emperor Isaac II Angelos, whose son Alexios IV promised financial and military aid. When the payment did not come, the crusaders captured and plundered the city in April 1204. The leaders of the crusade, among them Boniface I of Montferrat, and the Republic of Venice had planned a Latin Empire to replace the Byzantine Empire as the Western-recognized Roman Empire in the east.

On 9 May 1204 Baldwin IX of Flanders was elected emperor with Venetian support and crowned as Baldwin I on 16 May in the Hagia Sophia, in a ceremony that closely followed Eastern Roman practice. In the Partitio terrarum imperii Romaniae of 1 October 1204, three eighths of the empire, including Crete, went to Venice. The empire claimed the rest, with vassal fiefs in Greece: the Kingdom of Thessalonica, the Principality of Achaea, the Duchy of Athens and the Duchy of the Archipelago. The name "Latin Empire" was given by historians in the 16th century; its own documents called it the imperium Constantinopolitanum, and the Byzantines spoke of the Frankokratia.
sections.socioeconomy:
The Latins did not trust the professional Greek bureaucracy and dismantled the Greek economic administration of the lands they took. The result was disastrous, disrupting production and trade, and almost from its start the empire was asking the papacy for aid. For a few years Thrace exported wheat and furs, and Constantinople still profited from its place on major trade routes. After the death of Henry of Flanders in 1216 there was a major deficit in leadership, and by the 1230s the city, its population drastically reduced, faced a shortage of basic foodstuffs.

In several senses the only significant export was the sale to Western Europe of relics looted from Greek churches. The elite were Frankish and Venetian lords, headed by the emperor, the barons and lower vassals, among them many former Byzantine aristocrats. The bulk of the people were Orthodox Greeks, still divided by the Byzantine system into income classes based on land. Known artwork made within the empire is almost non-existent, but crusader rule made Byzantine art better known in Italy and contributed to the Italo-Byzantine style.
sections.military:
In Asia Minor the crusaders took most of Bithynia by 1205, defeating Theodore I Laskaris at Poemanenum and Prusa. A truce with Nicaea followed in 1207, a further Latin victory at the Rhyndakos river in October 1211, and the Treaty of Nymphaeum in 1214. In Europe the empire met a powerful enemy at once. At the Battle of Adrianople on 14 April 1205 the Bulgarian tsar Kaloyan and his Cuman allies crushed the Latin heavy cavalry and captured Emperor Baldwin, who died in prison in Tarnovo.

Henry of Flanders recovered most of Thrace and campaigned in Macedonia, Thessaly and Central Greece against the Lombard lords of Thessalonica. The Despotate of Epirus under Theodore Komnenos Doukas captured and executed Peter of Courtenay, took Thessalonica in 1224 and conquered Thrace in 1225–26, reaching Constantinople itself. In 1224 the Latins were defeated at the battle of Poimanenon and lost nearly all of Asia. In 1235 Nicaea and Bulgaria besieged Constantinople without success. After the Nicaean victory at the Battle of Pelagonia in 1259, only the Theodosian walls stood between Michael VIII Palaiologos and the city.
sections.governance:
The empire was formed and run on Western European feudal principles, with some elements of the Byzantine bureaucracy. The emperor was assisted by a council of the barons, the Venetian Podestà of Constantinople and his six-member council. This council had a major voice in government, above all during regencies, when the Regent (moderator imperii) depended on its consent. The podestà was practically independent of the emperor, ruling the Venetian quarters of Constantinople and Pera and Venice's dominions; he was styled Governor of One-Fourth and One-Half of the Empire of Romania and wore the imperial crimson buskins.

Baldwin's title closely copied that of the Byzantine emperors, and Henry's letters used three versions, Emperor of Romania, of the Romans and of Constantinople. After Henry died in 1216 came Peter of Courtenay, his widow Yolanda of Flanders, the regents Conon de Béthune and Cardinal Giovanni Colonna, Robert of Courtenay, the regent John of Brienne and Baldwin II. A Latin Catholic hierarchy was set up under the Latin patriarch of Constantinople; Greek bishops who accepted papal supremacy kept their sees, and Greek priests served the Orthodox majority in a subordinate position.
sections.impact:
The founding of the Latin Empire created five polities at once that claimed to be the Roman Empire: the Latin Empire, the Holy Roman Empire, the Despotate of Epirus, the Empire of Nicaea and the Empire of Trebizond. Possession of Constantinople was the key claim that set the Latin emperors apart from the Byzantine rivals in Nicaea, Trebizond and Thessalonica. Western sources and the papacy treated the conquest as a takeover of the eastern empire, not its replacement; a German chronicle of the time, the Deeds of the Bishops of Halberstadt, called Baldwin "emperor of the Greeks".

The empire never gained political or economic dominance over the other Latin powers set up on former Byzantine land, above all Venice, which drew lasting profit from its share. Western religious orders, the Cistercians, Franciscans and Dominicans, founded houses in the empire, and disputes with the Greek clergy over ordination, jurisdiction and tithes continued. Through the relics and icons carried west, crusader rule over Constantinople fed the Italo-Byzantine style of painting, as in Berlinghiero's Virgin and Child of c. 1230, modelled on the Hodegetria icon type.
sections.decline:
After Robert of Courtenay died in 1228, a regency under John of Brienne ruled. The Epirote threat ended with Epirus's defeat by the Bulgarians at the Battle of Klokotnitsa, but Nicaea took its place. In 1237 Baldwin II came of age and took over a much-diminished state. He travelled often to Western Europe seeking aid, largely without success, and raised money by selling the lead roofs of the Great Palace and pledging his son Philip to Venetian merchants. By 1247 the Nicaeans had effectively surrounded the emperor's main holdings in Europe.

An attempt on Constantinople failed in 1260. In March 1261 Michael VIII Palaiologos made an alliance with Genoa. The general Alexios Strategopoulos, sent with 800 soldiers, most of them Cumans, learned at Selymbria that the Latin garrison and the Venetian fleet were away raiding Daphnousia. On the night of 24/25 July 1261 his men entered through a secret passage and opened a gate. Baldwin II and the Latin inhabitants fled by ship, and the Byzantine Empire was restored. The imperial title passed to Philip of Courtenay and to the Angevin princes of Taranto, and other Latin states in Greece lasted, some until the 18th century.

summary: The Latin Empire was the Crusader state set up in Constantinople after the Fourth Crusade sacked the city in 1204. Ruled on feudal lines and overshadowed by Venice, it lost ground to Bulgaria, Epirus and Nicaea year by year until a small Nicaean force retook the city in 1261 and restored the Byzantine Empire.
references: Lock, Peter, The Franks in the Aegean, 1204–1500 (Routledge, 2014)

pointDescs.1204: The crusaders take Constantinople, crown Baldwin I and divide the Byzantine lands, with vassal states across Greece.
pointDescs.1205: Baldwin I is captured by Kaloyan at the Battle of Adrianople, though most of Bithynia is taken in Asia Minor.
pointDescs.1210: Henry of Flanders recovers most of Thrace and makes peace with Bulgaria by marrying Maria of Bulgaria.
pointDescs.1214: The Treaty of Nymphaeum recognizes Latin control of most of Bithynia and Mysia.
pointDescs.1216: Henry dies at Thessalonica, and the empire loses its most capable ruler.
pointDescs.1224: Defeat at Poimanenon costs nearly all of Asia, and Thessalonica falls to Epirus.
pointDescs.1225: Epirote armies conquer Thrace in 1225–26 and appear before Constantinople.
pointDescs.1228: Robert of Courtenay dies and a regency under John of Brienne is set up.
pointDescs.1235: The last Latin possessions in Asia fall to Nicaea, and a Nicaean and Bulgarian siege of Constantinople fails.
pointDescs.1237: Baldwin II takes over a much-diminished state and seeks aid in the West.
pointDescs.1259: The Nicaean victory at Pelagonia leaves only the city's walls in Michael VIII's way.
pointDescs.1261: Alexios Strategopoulos enters Constantinople on 24/25 July and Baldwin II flees.

notes: The article's bibliography lists only Lock; no other references given.
The article says the Bulgarian threat was defeated in a victory 'the following year' after 1207, undated; left undated.
Point strengths are judgement: the peak placed at the founding and under Henry.
